statement: Whether a tablet's logo or look tells what it holds has not been measured directly in the studies read: none compared the contents of tablets that share a logo, and the 99% reliability that the Dutch Drug Information and Monitoring System (DIMS) states for identifying tablets by their look is given without data. The nearest evidence comes from the Netherlands. DIMS staff compared 471 online reports about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market, posted on Pillreports.net (218) and Partyflock.nl (253) between January 2014 and December 2015, each with the laboratory results (gas chromatography–mass spectrometry) of tablets fitting its description that had been handed in at Dutch test offices within 12 weeks before or after it. 39.7 in 100 reports (95% CI 35.2 to 44.4) stated an amount of MDMA more than 10 mg above the laboratory value and 17.6 in 100 (14.0 to 21.2) more than 10 mg below it, so that stated amounts were on average 10.6 mg too high (6.7 to 14.4); 15.5 in 100 (12.3 to 18.9) left out a substance that matching tablets contained. How many reports were within 10 mg is not given (at most 42.7 in 100, editors' calculation by subtraction). The authors scored 15.3 in 100 (11.9 to 18.5) as 'dangerous': the amount stated more than 40 mg too low (10.2 in 100), or a psychoactive substance left out in amounts they call relevant without defining them in numbers (7.0 in 100). Stating too much MDMA, the commonest error, was not scored as dangerous: the authors considered it and judged its risk too speculative. In 10.8 in 100 reports the description fitted more than one distinct tablet in the database, which the authors take to mean that several different pills on the market fitted it; reports with a picture fitted more than one tablet less often (odds ratio 0.298, 0.111 to 0.799) but were not less often 'dangerous' (1.044, 0.490 to 2.225). Reports that gave a range of amounts instead of one figure were 'dangerous' less often: 38 of 312 (12.2 in 100) against 34 of 159 without a range (21.4 in 100), an editors' reconstruction from the printed percentages and site totals that reproduces the paper's chi-square of 6.890. The paper calls reports without a range 'approximately twice as likely' to be dangerous; that is the odds ratio (1/0.511, about 1.96), while one proportion is about 1.76 times the other (editors' calculation). The authors suggest, without testing it, that pills that look alike can come from different batches or makers, with different amounts or even different substances, and that people may post amounts guessed from their own experience, or sellers post high ones to advertise; reports that named DIMS laboratory tests as their source often gave amounts that were not in its database (no count given), and reports often named no source at all (Vrolijk et al., 2017). Because each report was compared with tablets of matching description rather than with the tablet it was about, a mismatch may come from a wrong report or from a look-alike tablet with other contents, and the study cannot tell these apart (editors' reading). Some people feel little from a pill that a report called strong: reports stating too much MDMA, the commonest error here, fit one possible reason, but these studies did not look at other reasons, such as tolerance, or at what happens when people then take more. The system's own authors report, without counts, that in the second half of the 2000s tablets sold as ecstasy often held 2C-B instead, and that these highly resembled ecstasy tablets, with similar logos, shapes and colours; amphetamine, too, turns up in tablets with logos like those of ecstasy (Brunt & Niesink, 2011). At most Dutch test offices, staff identify some tablets on the spot: they record the logo, shape, colour, weight, diameter (matched to within 0.10 mm) and thickness (within 0.30 mm), do a Marquis colour test, and look for a match on a list, updated weekly, of tablets recently analysed in the laboratory; a recognised tablet is given its batch's average MDMA content without a new analysis, and tablets not recognised, or in doubt, go to the laboratory. On average 30 in 100 tablets were identified this way. The papers say that a recognised tablet's average content (and, in one, its variation) is then known, but report neither, and that checks of recognised tablets that people still had analysed showed 99% reliability, without numbers, period or what counted as right (the main substance or the amount) (Vogels et al., 2009; Brunt & Niesink, 2011); a later report from seven European drug-checking services calls the method very reliable in the Netherlands, citing those two papers (Brunt et al., 2017). Over the years, among 33,006 tablets sold as ecstasy that people handed in at Dutch test offices in 1993–2008 and that were analysed in the laboratory (tablets identified by look and not sent to the laboratory are not among them), the share holding only MDMA as the active drug ranged from 44 in 100 in 1997 to 86 in 100 on average in 2000–2004; the yearly median of MDMA in a tablet ranged from 60 mg (1998) to 84 mg (1994), and single tablets held from traces (under 1 mg) to 225 mg (Vogels et al., 2009). These are amounts measured in tablets, not amounts to take. By the system's authors' statements, which give no counts, only 30 in 100 tablets handed in during October 1997 held MDMA or a similar drug, and only 40 in 100 in March 2009 held MDMA (Brunt & Niesink, 2011). What tablets sold as ecstasy held at seven European drug-checking services in 2008–2013 is in the answer on whether ecstasy is really MDMA. All four papers are by, or led by, the team that runs DIMS, whose database is the reference in the online study. The tablets are those people chose to bring in, which the authors think over-represents tablets whose effects were not what people expected. The online study covers two websites in one country over two years; it gives no count of reports found, excluded or left without a matching tablet, does not say how a value was chosen when several tablets matched or whether the scorers agreed, and defines 'dangerous' differently in its abstract, methods and discussion; its authors caution that people in the Netherlands may be better informed about drug content than elsewhere. The only source these papers cite for how much tablets of the same appearance vary (Cole et al., 2002) was not read. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Can a pill's logo or look tell you what's in it? Nobody has shown that it can: no study here measured how much pills with the same logo differ. Staff of the Dutch drug-checking system compared 471 online reports about ecstasy pills, from two websites in 2014 and 2015, with lab results for pills matching each report's description. About 40 in 100 reports said more than 10 mg more MDMA than the lab found, about 18 in 100 said more than 10 mg less, and about 16 in 100 left out another drug. The authors called 15 in 100 dangerous (far too little MDMA stated, or a drug left out); saying too much, the commonest mistake, wasn't counted. A photo helped match a report to the right pill but didn't make it less often dangerous. Reports giving a range of amounts were dangerous less often: 12 in 100, against 21 in 100 for one figure. An overstated report may be one reason some people feel little from a pill; nobody here looked at other reasons, or at what happens when people then take more. The same testers say pills that looked like ecstasy, with similar logos, have held 2C-B or amphetamine. They identify some pills by exact size, weight, logo and a colour test, against pills lab-tested in recent weeks, and call this 99% reliable, but have published no data for it. In lab tests of Dutch pills sold as ecstasy from 1993 to 2008, only MDMA was found in 44 in 100 in 1997 and about 86 in 100 in 2000–2004, and single pills held from a trace to 225 mg (lab amounts, not amounts to take). All of this is Dutch, from the team that runs the testing.
population: Online reports about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market posted on Pillreports.net (218) and Partyflock.nl (253) between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2015 (471 reports; who posted them is unknown); tablets sold as ecstasy that people handed in at Dutch DIMS test offices, 33,006 of them analysed in the laboratory in 1993–2008, with the system's statements to July 2010; and the identification of tablets by look at Dutch test offices and, as described, at European drug-checking services in 2008–2013
exposure: A tablet's logo and other visible features (shape, colour, size, weight): as described, with or without a picture, in online reports; and as used, with a Marquis colour test, by Dutch test-office staff to recognise tablets on a weekly updated list of tablets recently analysed in the laboratory
comparator: Laboratory analysis of tablets handed in to DIMS (gas chromatography–mass spectrometry and other methods): for online reports, tablets fitting the report's description handed in within 12 weeks before or after it, not the tablet the report described; no study compared tablets that share a logo with each other, and the validation data for recognition by look are unpublished
outcome: Share of online reports whose stated MDMA amount was more than 10 mg above or below (or more than 40 mg below) the laboratory value for matching tablets, that left out substances found in them, or that the authors scored as 'dangerous'; share whose description fitted more than one distinct tablet; report features (picture, range of amounts) associated with 'dangerous' reports; look-alike tablets holding other drugs (no counts); share of tablets identified by look and its stated reliability; content of laboratory-analysed tablets sold as ecstasy by year (share with only MDMA; MDMA per tablet)
magnitude: Vrolijk et al. (2017): 471 online reports (Pillreports.net 218, Partyflock.nl 253), 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2015, each compared with DIMS laboratory records (GC–MS) of tablets fitting its description handed in within 12 weeks before or after it; percentages with 95% bootstrap CIs (1,000 samples; Table 1): MDMA stated more than 10 mg too high 39.7% (35.2–44.4; Pillreports 47.7, Partyflock 32.8; χ² 10.86, P = 0.001); more than 10 mg too low 17.6% (14.0–21.2); more than 40 mg too low 10.2% (7.6–13.0); unreported substance 15.5% (12.3–18.9); unreported substance scored dangerous 7.0% (4.7–9.3); 'dangerous' overall 15.3% (11.9–18.5); mean difference 10.6 mg too high (6.7–14.4); within 10 mg or no amount given: not reported, at most 42.7% (editors' calculation, 100 − 39.7 − 17.6). Multiple database hits 10.8% (8.1–13.6); picture included 46.9% (42.3–51.2); picture with multiple hits Exp(b) 0.298 (0.111–0.799), P = 0.016; multiple hits with more than 40 mg too low 4.880 (1.608–14.81), P = 0.005, and with an unreported substance 2.556 (1.056–6.186), P = 0.037; multiple hits with 'dangerous' χ² 34.26, P < 0.001; picture with 'dangerous' 1.044 (0.490–2.225), P = 0.912. Range given in 66.2% (61.8–70.1); range with 'dangerous' Exp(b) 0.511 (0.307–0.850), P = 0.010; Pearson χ² 6.890 (printed P 0.007). Editors' reconstruction from Table 1 and the site totals (range 148 + 164 = 312, none 159; 'dangerous' 32 + 40 = 72; data/verification/pdf-2026-11-26/754_calculations.py): 'dangerous' in 34 of 159 reports without a range (21.4%) and 38 of 312 with one (12.2%), the only split that gives Pearson χ² 6.890; ratio of proportions about 1.76, odds ratio about 1.96 (= 1/0.511), the paper's 'approximately twice as likely'. Vogels et al. (2009): 33,006 laboratory-analysed tablets sold as ecstasy, 1993–2008; only MDMA as active substance 44% (1997) to 86% on average (2000–2004); median MDMA per tablet 73 mg over the period, yearly 60 mg (1998) to 84 mg (1994); single tablets from under 1 mg (traces) to 225 mg (tablet contents, not doses). Identification by look and a Marquis test against a weekly list: on average 30% of tablets; reliability stated as 99% from internal checks, without data (Vogels et al., 2009; Brunt & Niesink, 2011); called very reliable in the Netherlands, citing those two papers (Brunt et al., 2017). Brunt & Niesink (2011): tablets with MDMA or an MDMA-like substance 30% in October 1997 and tablets with MDMA 40% in March 2009 (monthly lows, no denominators); 2C-B in tablets resembling ecstasy, with similar logos, shapes and colours, in the second half of the 2000s, and amphetamine in tablets with logos similar to ecstasy (no counts). No paper reports how content varied among tablets sharing a logo.

evidence.locator: Author affiliations (p. 94); Materials and methods › Design, single paragraph (p. 95); Procedure: comparison to the DIMS database, single paragraph (p. 95); Measures: scoring method, single paragraph (pp. 95–96)
evidence.extracted: 471 online reports about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market, posted on Pillreports.net (218) and Partyflock.nl (253) from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2015, the two sites earlier DIMS monitoring found most active on ecstasy tablets; collected by hand, with each report's stated content, physical description, picture and date archived. DIMS employees compared each report with DIMS database records (GC–MS composition, physical characteristics, date and place of submission) of the tablet within 12 weeks before or after the report's date. Stated MDMA was scored too high or too low if more than 10 mg from the database value (for a range, its average); 'unreported substance' if similar database tablets in the window held substances the report did not mention; 'dangerous' if stated more than 40 mg too low (for a range, its average 40 mg too low or its maximum 40 mg below the database maximum) or if an unreported substance was psychoactive and present in relevant concentrations (not defined in numbers). The comparison rested only on the report's own information, so a poorly described tablet matched several distinct database tablets ('multiple database hits'), which the authors take to mean that several pills on the market fitted the description and a reader could not tell them apart from the report. All four authors are at the Trimbos Institute, which runs DIMS.

risk_of_bias.note: The online-report study (card sc_vrolijk_2017: JBI moderate) does not say how many reports were found, excluded or left without a matching tablet, how a comparison value was chosen when several tablets matched (10.8 in 100 reports), or how many scorers there were, whether they were blind and whether they agreed; its reference is a database of tablets matched by description within 12 weeks, not the tablet each report described; and 'dangerous' is defined three ways, with 'relevant' amounts never in numbers. The monitoring data (cards sc_vogels_2009 and sc_brunt_2011: JBI moderate; sc_brunt_2017: high as a measure of markets) are tablets people chose to bring in, exclude tablets identified by look, and rest their stated reliability on unpublished checks. All four papers are by, or led by, the team that runs the reference system. One level, not two: the main percentages come from a laboratory-based reference with tight intervals, and these problems could shift them but are unlikely to reverse the pattern (frequent errors, more overstatement than understatement).

inconsistency.note: One study for the accuracy of online reports; the monitoring papers agree that tablets sold as ecstasy varied widely in content from year to year, and none contradicts the online study.

indirectness.note: No study measured what the question asks: whether tablets that share a logo or look hold the same drug and amount. The online study measures how well posted descriptions matched laboratory records of tablets fitting the same description, which mixes wrong reports with look-alike tablets that differ, and the tablets the reports were about were never tested; the monitoring data describe tablets in general, not tablets that share a logo. All data are Dutch (1993–2015), where a national testing system may make online information better than elsewhere (the authors' caution).

imprecision.note: 471 reports; the main percentages have 95% intervals about 3 to 5 points either side. The look-alike statements and the monthly lows have no counts and are worded as the authors' statements; they do not carry the rating.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study and one monitoring series; the authors describe the online study as the first of its kind.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (shares of online reports and of tablets): starts low and is never upgraded; risk of bias −1 and indirectness −1 (see the domain notes); very low. It is not rated as a test-accuracy study (METHODS 6.3): an online report is not a test, and the laboratory reference was not applied to the tablet each report described. Status single study: the accuracy of online reports rests on one study; Vogels et al. (2009), Brunt and Niesink (2011) and Brunt et al. (2017) are successive publications of the same Dutch monitoring system and team (Brunt is an author of all four papers, Niesink of three), describe other things (what tablets held; how tablets are identified by look) and do not replicate it. The answer to the question, that nobody has shown that a logo or look tells what a tablet holds, rests on the absence of a study, not on a finding against it: the Dutch system's recognition by measurements, logo and a colour test against recently analysed tablets is not shown to be unreliable either, but its reliability is unpublished (editors' reading). The 21 against 12 in 100 is an editors' reconstruction that reproduces the paper's chi-square exactly; the paper's 'approximately twice as likely' is the odds ratio. Rule 0 ('I barely felt it'): the statement names overstated reports as one possible reason someone felt little from a pill and says these studies did not look at other reasons or at what happens when people then take more; it gives no advice, and the amounts are tablet contents, not doses.
